modules.title: 4-bit Mini ALU
modules.summary: Additional exercise: a 4-bit ALU selecting add/sub/AND/XOR via a 2-bit OP code, with carry, overflow, zero, and negative flags. Your task — no reference code shown; test your own against a real simulator below.
modules.statement:
Design and implement a 4-bit Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) using Verilog HDL. The ALU takes two 4-bit inputs A and B and a 2-bit control input OP. Based on the value of OP, the ALU should perform one of the following operations:

OPOperation
00A + B
01A − B
10A AND B
11A XOR B

The ALU should generate a 4-bit output Result along with the following status flags:

  • C — carry-out flag for arithmetic operations
  • V — signed overflow flag
  • Z — zero flag, set to 1 when Result = 0000
  • N — negative flag, equal to the most significant bit of Result

Use the modules developed in today's lab wherever possible. In particular, reuse your 4-bit adder/subtractor module for arithmetic operations and use multiplexing logic to select the required result.

module ALU4(Result, C, V, Z, N, A, B, OP);

input [3:0] A, B;
input [1:0] OP;

output [3:0] Result;
output C, V, Z, N;

Write an appropriate testbench to verify all four ALU operations. Your test cases should also include at least one example each for: carry generation, signed overflow, zero result, and negative result.

Bonus: extend the ALU by adding OR, left-shift, right-shift, and signed comparison operations using a 3-bit control input.
modules.signature: module ALU4(Result, C, V, Z, N, A, B, OP);

modules.title: D Flip-Flop — Synchronous Clear (Active Low)
modules.summary: As given in the lab sheet (module dff_sync_clear). Clear only takes effect on the next clock edge, not the instant clearb goes low.

waveform.note: Watch clearb drop at t=18 — q doesn't react until the next rising clock edge at t=25. That's the defining trait of a synchronous clear: it's just another data input to the always block, sampled only at the clock edge like d is.

modules.title: D Flip-Flop — Asynchronous Clear (Active Low)
modules.summary: As given in the lab sheet (module dff_async_clear). Clear reacts immediately, without waiting for a clock edge.

waveform.note: Watch clearb drop at t=18 — q reacts immediately, no clock edge needed. Compare with the synchronous version above, which held q until t=25. That immediate reaction (clearb is in the always block's sensitivity list alongside the clock) is what makes a clear asynchronous.

modules.title: D Flip-Flop — Synchronous Clear (Active High)
modules.summary: Same synchronous behavior as dff_sync_clear_low, but clear is asserted with a 1 instead of a 0 — a common source of confusion when reusing someone else's DFF module.

waveform.note: Same q trace as the active-low synchronous version — only the meaning of the clear signal's value flips (asserted = 1 here, not 0). Sync vs. async is about the sensitivity list; active-high vs. active-low is just which value of clear means "clear now".

modules.title: D Flip-Flop — Asynchronous Clear (Active High)
modules.summary: Combines the two traits: reacts immediately (asynchronous) and is asserted by a 1 (active high).

waveform.note: Immediate reaction like the other async version, but asserted by clear=1. Four variants, two independent choices — sync vs. async decides *when* the DFF checks clear; active-high vs. active-low decides *which value* of clear means clear.

modules.title: Non-blocking Assignment (<=) — a real 3-stage pipeline
modules.summary: A chain of three registers, in -> q1 -> q2 -> out, each stage updated with <=. Compare with the Blocking Assignment card below — same in/clk stimulus, dramatically different timing.

waveform.note: With <=, every right-hand side is read using the value each register held BEFORE this clock edge — all three reads happen first, then all three writes land together. So a new value of in takes exactly one clock edge to reach q1, one more to reach q2, one more to reach out: a genuine 3-stage pipeline. Watch in rise at t=3 — out only follows 3 edges later, at t=25.

modules.title: Blocking Assignment (=) — the pipeline collapses
modules.summary: The exact same three statements, in -> q1 -> q2 -> out, but with = instead of <=. Same in/clk stimulus as the Non-blocking card above — watch how differently out behaves.

waveform.note: With =, each statement takes effect immediately, so the very next line reads the value that was just written. q1 = in updates q1 right away; q2 = q1 then reads that brand-new q1; out = q2 then reads that brand-new q2 — all three registers snap to in's value within the same clock edge, same simulation instant. The intended 3-stage shift register has collapsed into something that just mirrors in, one edge late. This is why non-blocking (<=) is the rule for clocked always blocks: blocking (=) here silently destroys the pipeline structure without any error or warning.

modules.title: Generating a Clock in Verilog
modules.summary: A testbench has no physical oscillator — you write a small always/forever block that flips a reg on a fixed delay. Three equivalent idioms, shown below.
modules.statement:
All three of these produce the identical clock waveform above — pick whichever reads clearest in your testbench.

1. forever + toggle (what the lab sheet uses)
initial begin
  clk = 0;
  forever #5 clk = ~clk;
end
2. always block (no forever needed — always already repeats)
initial clk = 0;
always #5 clk = ~clk;
3. parameterized period (change one number to change speed)
parameter PERIOD = 10;
initial clk = 0;
always #(PERIOD/2) clk = ~clk;

All three run forever, so your testbench needs its own $finish (usually after some fixed delay, or after a loop of N clock edges) — otherwise the simulation never ends.
modules.signature: initial begin clk = 0; forever #5 clk = ~clk; end

waveform.note: clk starts at 0, then flips every 5 time units forever, giving a period of 10 and a 50% duty cycle — the exact idiom the Lab 3 sheet uses in its own DFF testbench.

modules.title: Sequential Block (begin ... end) — delays add up
modules.summary: Statements inside begin/end run one after another. Each #delay is measured from when the PREVIOUS statement finished, so the delays accumulate.
modules.signature: initial begin #5 a=1; #10 b=0; #15 c=1; end

waveform.note: a changes at t=5 (5). b changes at t=5+10=15 (not t=10!). c changes at t=15+15=30. Each delay counts from where the previous line left off — that's what "sequential" means here.

modules.title: Parallel Block (fork ... join) — delays race from the same start line
modules.summary: Same three statements, same three delays as the Sequential Block card above — but inside fork/join every #delay is measured from the moment the fork started, not from the previous statement.
modules.signature: initial fork #5 a=1; #10 b=0; #15 c=1; join

waveform.note: a changes at t=5, b at t=10, c at t=15 — all measured from t=0, running side by side. Compare with the Sequential Block card: same numbers, but b lands at t=10 here vs t=15 there, and c lands at t=15 here vs t=30 there. fork/join finishes as soon as its LAST branch completes (t=15), not one accumulated total.

modules.title: Mealy Machine FSM
modules.summary: A 3-state Mealy machine (as given in the lab sheet): output depends on both the current state AND the current input, so outp can change the instant inp does — not just on clock edges.

waveform.note: state is registered (updates only on posedge clk or posedge rst) but outp is assigned combinationally within that same case — so watch how state visibly steps through 00 -> 01/10 -> ... on each clock edge, feeding the fixed test sequence 0101_0111_0111_0010 (LSB first) one bit per edge. This is the lab sheet's own deterministic test loop — the $random-based extra loop from the sheet is left out here so the trace is reproducible.

modules.title: 4-bit Shift Register
modules.summary: A 4-bit right shift register (as given in the lab sheet): on every clock edge, when EN=1, in is shifted into the top bit and every other bit slides one position down; the bottom bit is dropped.

waveform.note: Q starts at 4'd10 = 4'b1010. While EN=1, each posedge sets Q to {in, Q[3:1]} — in becomes the new bit 3, and the old bit 0 falls off the end. While EN=0, Q holds. Note this always block uses = (blocking) rather than <= — with only one statement per edge here that's harmless, but see the Blocking vs. Non-blocking cards above for why that stops being true the moment a second statement is added.
